extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy interested in pragmatism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying William James's pragmatic criteria for judging truth, hypotheses, and metaphysical notions (as presented in a lecture on pragmatism). Focuses on how ideas are evaluated by their practical effects and relations to experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: New truth as additive vs. rearranging
rubrics_metrics.description: A new fact may simply be added to experience without altering old beliefs, or it may oblige a rearrangement of existing beliefs; how a new opinion counts as 'true' depends on how well it assimilates the novel to the stock of beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: simple numerical addition of facts (day follows day) vs. disruptive examples like 'radium' which appeared to violate conservation of energy until reinterpreted (discovery of helium) permitted minimum alteration. The new idea that best satisfies both leaning on old truth and grasping new fact is the truest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as the marriage-function between old beliefs and new facts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no purely objective, non-human truth; 'to be true' means to perform the function of mediating between earlier truths and newer observations — truth is what successfully performs this marriage-function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth is judged by its human role in assimilating experience; the lecture emphasizes that so-called objective truth is often the 'dead heart' of living truth and that even ancient truths have been reinterpreted pragmatically (logical/mathematical transformations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatist test: truth is what 'works' in experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The probable truth of an idea is judged by the practical working-values it yields in experience — the test of probable truth is 'what works best in the way of leading us' and what 'fits every part of life best.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with rationalism's demand for absolute correspondence; pragmatism prefers concreteness and observable effects. The lecture repeatedly uses metaphors (tree grafting, cash-value) to show truth is measured by practical success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as a species of the good — 'cash-value' criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: THE TRUE IS THE NAME OF WHATEVER PROVES ITSELF TO BE GOOD IN THE WAY OF BELIEF, and good for definite, assignable reasons; truth is one species of good rather than a category apart from good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If belief in an idea benefits life (unless it incidentally clashes with greater benefits), it counts as true to that extent. The lecture gives moral-holiday example for the Absolute: true 'in so far forth' as it affords comfort and permits relaxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic restriction of hypotheses to their practical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The legitimate content of hypotheses should be limited to the practical consequences they have for future experience; hypotheses carry 'supernumerary features' which can be legitimately discarded if they produce no pragmatic difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the belief in the Absolute may be restricted to its holiday-giving value to avoid clashes with other beliefs. Pragmatism 'unstiffens' theories by allowing hypotheses only their cash-value in experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence-of-theories test when no future consequences differ
rubrics_metrics.description: If two rival theories (e.g., materialism vs theism) lead to identical consequences for all possible future experience (or the world is completed), the dispute between them is purely verbal and pragmatically irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: imagine the world complete and finished — the theist and materialist explanations yield the same past facts and no difference in future experience, so the pragmatist treats them as meaning the same thing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatism demands discernible practical issues in metaphysical debates
rubrics_metrics.description: Every genuine metaphysical dispute must involve some practical issue or conjectural practical consequences; without possible alternative practical outcomes, philosophical disputes are mere verbalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture argues that metaphysicians who cannot point to different practical outcomes are engaged in 'pompous trifling' and that scientists/positivists rightly ignore disputes with no pragmatic differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-mindedness to hypotheses with practical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Pragmatism will entertain any hypothesis and consider any evidence so long as the hypothesis has practical consequences—no rigid preconceptions about what counts as proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pragmatism is described as 'completely genial' and 'democratic' — it accepts logic, senses, mysticism, and humble private experiences provided they have practical bearings; it widens the field of search for truth (and for God) accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting of mystical or personal experiences only by their consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystical or intensely personal experiences are admissible evidence for pragmatism provided they have observable practical consequences in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James notes pragmatism 'will count mystical experiences if they have practical consequences' and will take a God who 'lives in the very dirt of private fact' if that notion proves pragmatically useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance as pragmatic/cash-value notion (nominalist reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'substance' names a group of attributes (cash-value) rather than an inaccessible bearer behind attributes; nominalists claim substance is merely a convenient name for a cohesion of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include blackboard crayon and chalk: what we know are the attributes (whiteness, friability). The Eucharist dispute is offered as the one major case where a real substance-change (substance separated from accidents) would have pragmatic importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal identity defined pragmatically in terms of memory/consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal identity consists in 'so much consciousness' — the continuity of remembered experiences; identity is pragmatically relevant for the justice of reward and punishment because accountability depends on consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke's examples: if a person has no consciousness of past deeds, punishing them is equivalent to creating misery; thus identity is a practical matter grounded in verifiable memory-links rather than a metaphysical soul-substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materialism vs spiritualism judged by future practical differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the world is 'run by matter' or 'run by spirit/God' is pragmatically indifferent to the past but becomes a significant practical question only insofar as the alternative hypotheses imply different future programs or consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the world is unfinished (has a future), belief in divine providence vs blind atoms may direct different actions or expectations; if no future differences are deducible, the debate is idle.
